intro: Two sides of the same thing: being in the photos, and getting paid to take them.

posts.title: Stop handing your phone to strangers
posts.author: Personal Paparazzi
posts.summary: The photo you get back is blurry, tilted, and missing your feet. Here is why that keeps happening, and what to do instead.
posts.body:
You are somewhere worth remembering. You look around, pick the friendliest face, and hand over your phone.

What comes back is almost never what you wanted. The framing is tight, so the place you travelled to is a smudge behind your head. The focus is on the wall. Somebody blinked. And you cannot ask for another one without feeling rude, so you say thank you and walk away with it.

## Why it goes wrong

The stranger is doing you a favour, and favours are rushed. They take one photo, not fifteen. They stand where they were already standing rather than backing up. They do not know that the fountain behind you is the whole point.

## What to do instead

Ask for the shot you want before you hand the phone over. Say where to stand. Say what should be in the frame behind you. Ask for three, not one.

Or send a request in the app and let somebody who does this on purpose take them.

posts.title: How to be in your own holiday photos
posts.author: Personal Paparazzi
posts.summary: If you are the one who always takes the picture, you are in none of them. Four ways to fix that on your next trip.
posts.body:
Every family has one. The person who frames everybody up, counts to three, and then is missing from the entire album.

## Put the phone down first

Decide before the trip that there will be photos with you in them. It sounds obvious. It is the step everybody skips.

## Pick the moment, not the landmark

The photos people keep are rarely the posed one at the monument. They are the walk back, the laughing, the ice cream. Aim for those.

## Ask for movement

Standing still and smiling makes everybody look like a school portrait. Walk towards the camera. Turn around. Talk to each other.

## Get somebody else to take them

A request in the app takes a few seconds, and you end up in the photographs of your own holiday.

posts.title: Things to do in Nashville, and where the photo is worth taking
posts.author: Personal Paparazzi
posts.summary: Fifteen places people actually queue for, and what to do with your camera at each one.
posts.body:
Nashville takes about 16.9 million visitors a year, and most of them end up in the same handful of places. That is good news if you want a photograph, because it means somebody is always nearby.

## Broadway, the Honky Tonk Highway

Free live music every day of the year, from the morning until three in the morning. The neon is the photograph. Stand with your back to the bars so the signs are behind you rather than above your head.

## The John Seigenthaler Pedestrian Bridge

The clearest view of the skyline in the city, and no traffic to dodge. Go at the end of the day, when the light is behind the buildings.

## The Country Music Hall of Fame

About 1.6 million people a year go through it. The building itself photographs better than most of what is inside it.

## The Parthenon at Centennial Park

A full size replica of the Athenian original, with a 42 foot Athena inside. Stand far enough back that the columns are all in the frame.

## Cheekwood

Fifty five acres of garden on a 1920s estate. This is the one where you want somebody else holding the camera, because the scale of it does not survive a selfie.

posts.title: Your photos, your privacy
posts.author: Personal Paparazzi
posts.summary: What happens to the pictures after a stranger takes them, and what you are agreeing to.
posts.body:
Handing your camera to somebody is an act of trust, and it is worth knowing what happens next.

## The photos are yours

What you get from a session belongs to you. Personal Paparazzi, Inc. keeps no right to use your photos for commercial purposes without your explicit consent, and that is in the terms rather than only in a blog post.

## They come to you, not to a gallery

The photos upload at the end of the session and you download them to your own phone. There is no public album with your face in it.

## What you can ask for

You can ask for a shot to be retaken. You can say you would rather not be photographed from a particular angle. You can say when you are done. The person holding the camera is there for five minutes and the photos are the only reason.

## What we check

Every Personal Paparazzi passes an identity verification before they can accept sessions: we confirm they are who they say they are. We do not run criminal background checks, and we will not claim otherwise.

posts.title: Where to stand in Nashville on a Saturday
posts.author: Personal Paparazzi
posts.summary: Requests come from where the people are. Here is how the city sorts itself out across a weekend.
posts.body:
The difference between a slow afternoon and a busy one is rarely how good you are. It is where you were standing.

## Follow the footfall

Broadway takes most of the city's visitors, and it does not stop. If you want volume, that is where volume is.

## The quieter places are not worthless

The Hermitage sees about 190,000 people a year rather than millions, but the people who go there have planned the trip, and people who plan a trip want a photograph of it.

## Light beats footfall after five

Late in the day, the pedestrian bridge is worth more than a busier spot with worse light. You are selling a photograph, not proximity.

## Stay where you can be reached

A request goes to everybody nearby. Being fifteen minutes away is the same as not being there.

posts.title: The five minutes that make a good session
posts.author: Personal Paparazzi
posts.summary: You have got five minutes with people you have never met. Here is what to do with them.
posts.body:
A session is short. Most of what separates a good one from a bad one happens in the first thirty seconds.

## Say hello properly

A client who feels relaxed takes a better photo. Introduce yourself, say what is about to happen, and they stop bracing.

## Step back further than feels right

The reason they asked is the place they are standing in. If the frame is only faces, they could have done that themselves.

## Give one instruction at a time

Turn slightly left. Chin down a little. Walk towards me. People cannot process three at once, and they look stiff while they try.

## Take more than you need

Nine photos is the delivery, not the target. Shoot past it so they have a choice, and so one blink does not cost you the shot.

## Finish clearly

Tell them you are done and check they are happy before you walk away. That is the part they rate.

posts.title: Why we check who you are
posts.author: Personal Paparazzi
posts.summary: What the identity check covers, what it does not, and why it is the only thing standing between you and your first session.
posts.body:
Before you can accept sessions you pass an identity verification. It is the only check there is, and it is worth being precise about what that means.

## What it is

We confirm you are who you say you are. That is the whole check.

## What it is not

We do not run criminal background checks. We do not check employment history. We do not call references. If anybody tells a client otherwise, they are wrong, and we will not let that claim stand on our own site either.

We say this plainly because the alternative is worse. A safety promise we cannot keep is the most expensive kind of promise there is, and the first time it failed it would be your reputation in the story as much as ours.

## Why it helps you

Somebody is about to hand their phone, their family and four minutes of their holiday to a stranger who knocked on their afternoon. The check is small, but it is the difference between a platform and a classified ad, and it is part of why they press the button at all.

## What it costs you

Nothing, and a few minutes. There is no equipment to buy, no fee to join, and no portfolio to submit. You need to be 18 or older with a modern phone, and you need to be who you said you were.

posts.title: How many people come to Nashville, and where they all go
posts.author: Personal Paparazzi
posts.summary: 16.9 million visitors a year, and they are not spread evenly. The numbers behind where the requests come from.
posts.body:
Nashville takes about 16.9 million visitors a year. That number on its own is not much use to you. Where they go is.

## They concentrate

Most of those visitors end up on Broadway at some point. Free live music every day of the year, from the morning until three in the morning, and no ticket needed. That is why it sits at the top of the list in the earnings calculator.

## The paid attractions, in order

The Country Music Hall of Fame takes about 1.6 million a year. The Nashville Zoo at Grassmere takes over 1.4 million, which makes it the top paid attraction in Middle Tennessee. Cheekwood reaches up to 435,000 in a peak year. The Grand Ole Opry House sees over 250,000 on daytime tours alone, before the evening crowds. Andrew Jackson's Hermitage sees about 190,000.

## Small does not mean bad

The gap between 16.9 million and 190,000 looks decisive, and it is not the whole story. Somebody who drove out to the Hermitage planned that trip. People who plan a trip want a photograph of it. Broadway gives you volume; the quieter places give you people who already decided the day mattered.

## What we do not know yet

These are annual figures. We do not have reliable season by season numbers, so we are not going to invent them. When we have them, they go in the calculator and this post gets updated.

posts.title: How much can you make in a weekend
posts.author: Personal Paparazzi
posts.summary: The arithmetic, in full, with the parts we cannot promise marked as such.
posts.body:
The honest answer is that it depends on how many requests you accept and how busy it is where you are standing. That is not a dodge, so here is the arithmetic underneath it.

## What one session pays

A client pays $19.99 for a session: nine photos and one short video. You keep 50% of that, which is $10.00. Any tip is yours in full, on top. Earnings are deposited weekly, once the client receives their images.

## What a session costs you

Minutes. The session itself typically takes less than five. There is no gas to buy, no wear on your tires, and nothing to pay before you start, which is the part that separates this from driving.

## Doing the sum

At a busy spot, an estimated 6 to 10 sessions an hour is $60 to $100 an hour before tips. At a quieter one, an estimated 3 to 5 sessions is $30 to $50. Over a Saturday and a Sunday, eight hours each, the same arithmetic runs from a few hundred dollars to something over a thousand.

## The part we cannot promise

Those sessions an hour are estimated from how busy each place is. They are not measured, they are not an offer, and they are not a commitment to pay any amount. Nobody can tell you in advance how many people will press the button while you are standing there.

What we can tell you is the rate, which is fixed, and the time, which is short. The calculator on the sign-up page runs the sum for whichever place and however many hours you want to try.
